A1.1.1.q: An unhappy employee deletes key project files on their last day. Which internal threat is this?
A1.1.1.why: Insiders can damage systems on purpose or by mistake, including theft and installing unauthorised software.

A1.1.2.q: A burst pipe floods a server room and destroys the servers. How does Unit 2 classify this threat?
A1.1.2.why: Physical events, whether natural, accidental or deliberate, can damage IT systems and data.

A1.1.3.q: The server room is left unlocked and visitors walk around unescorted. What kind of weakness is this?
options: Weak security measures and unsafe practices
A1.1.3.why: Poor habits and weak controls make an organisation easier to attack.

A1.1.4.q: A manager writes the admin password on a sticky note on their monitor, and a visitor photographs it. Which threat is this?
A1.1.4.why: Data or logins exposed through human error, not a deliberate attack.

A1.2.1a.q: Opening an infected Word document runs hidden macro code that copies itself into other documents. What malware is this?
A1.2.1a.why: A virus attaches to a file and copies itself when the file is run.

A1.2.1b.q: Hidden software records every key a user presses and sends their bank passwords to a criminal. What is this?
A1.2.1b.why: Spyware secretly collects information about a user and sends it to a third party.

A1.2.1c.q: A free game fills the screen with pop-up adverts and installs an unwanted toolbar. What malware is this?
A1.2.1c.why: Adware displays or downloads adverts, from legitimate to deceptive.

A1.2.1d.q: All of a company's files are suddenly encrypted, and a note demands payment for the key. What malware is this?
A1.2.1d.why: Ransomware locks or encrypts data and demands payment.

A1.2.1e.q: Thousands of hijacked smart cameras are remotely ordered to flood a website with traffic. What are the cameras part of?
A1.2.1e.why: Bots are infected devices controlled remotely. Together they form a botnet, often used for DDoS.

A1.2.2.q: An attacker gets into a school database without permission and changes students' grades. Which threat is this?
A1.2.2.why: Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to systems or data.

A1.2.3.q: Attackers deliberately corrupt the data used to train a company's AI so that it makes bad decisions. Which threat is this?
A1.2.3.why: Sabotage is deliberately damaging or corrupting data, systems or infrastructure.

A1.2.4.q: Someone phones staff pretending to be from IT support and asks for their password to 'fix an issue'. Which threat is this?
A1.2.4.why: Social engineering tricks people, rather than technology, into giving away secure information.

A1.2.5.q: An intruder follows a member of staff through a secure door before it closes, without using a card. Which threat is this?
A1.2.5.why: Physical threats involve getting into secure areas, e.g. tailgating or shoulder surfing.

A1.3.1.q: Ransomware stops a factory's production line for three days, so no products are made. What kind of loss is this?
A1.3.1.why: Operational loss means the organisation can't operate or deliver its products and services.

A1.3.2.q: After a breach, a company pays a GDPR fine and refunds affected customers. What kind of loss is this?
A1.3.2.why: Financial loss is the money an incident costs: lost income, compensation and legal costs.

A1.3.3.q: News of a data breach trends on social media and customers post angry reviews. What kind of loss is this?
A1.3.3.why: Reputational loss is damage to how customers and the public see the organisation.

A1.3.4.q: A hacker steals the designs for a company's unreleased product and sells them to a rival. What kind of loss is this?
A1.3.4.why: IP loss is theft or exposure of an organisation's valuable ideas and secrets.

A1.4.1.q: A UK IT manager wants the latest official advice on a new ransomware strain affecting British businesses. Which source should they check first?
A1.4.1.why: The National Cyber Security Centre is the UK authority for threat reports and advice.

A1.4.2.q: A company follows a US government body's published standards for password policy. Which source is this?
A1.4.2.why: NIST is the US National Institute of Standards and Technology.

A1.4.3.q: A web developer checks a new site against a list of the most critical web application risks, such as injection. Which source is this?
A1.4.3.why: OWASP's Top 10 lists the most critical web application security risks.

A2.1.1.q: A port scan shows several firewall ports open that the business never uses. Which type of vulnerability is this?
A2.1.1.why: Network vulnerabilities include open firewall ports and external storage.

A2.1.2.q: Every member of staff has admin rights, and leavers' accounts are never disabled. Which type of vulnerability is this?
A2.1.2.why: Organisational vulnerabilities come from how permissions, passwords and accounts are managed.

A2.1.3.q: A company runs an unpatched web app that is open to SQL injection. Which type of vulnerability is this?
A2.1.3.why: Software vulnerabilities come from untrustworthy, outdated or badly made software.

A2.1.4.q: An office still runs a version of Windows that Microsoft no longer supports with security updates. Which type of vulnerability is this?
A2.1.4.why: OS weaknesses usually come from being outdated or misconfigured.

A2.1.5.q: Staff use old Android phones whose manufacturer has stopped sending security updates. Which type of vulnerability is this?
A2.1.5.why: Phones depend on their manufacturer (OEM) for updates, so they can be left unpatched.

A2.1.6.q: An unencrypted laptop is stolen from an employee's car. Which type of vulnerability did this exploit?
A2.1.6.why: Physical vulnerabilities allow theft of, or physical access to, equipment holding data.

A2.1.7.q: Two staff routinely share one login to save time, so no one can tell who did what. Which type of vulnerability is this?
A2.1.7.why: People-process vulnerabilities are weaknesses in how people actually use systems day to day.

A2.1.8.q: A smart CCTV camera with a default password is hijacked to spy on an office. Which security implication is this?
A2.1.8.why: Cloud services and IoT devices bring their own risks, such as default passwords and misconfiguration.

A2.2.q: An administrator wants to know if the router model they use has any newly found weaknesses. Where is a reliable source?
options: The manufacturer's website or security advisories
A2.2.why: Vulnerability information comes from manufacturers, advisories and professional security forums.

A2.3.q: An attacker in a car park gets into a company's systems through its poorly secured Wi-Fi. In risk terms, what is the Wi-Fi?
A2.3.why: An attack vector is the route an attacker uses to reach a system.

A2.4.q: Before attackers can, the IT team runs a tool that scans all devices for open ports and known weaknesses. What is this?
A2.4.why: Vulnerability assessment tools such as port scanners find weaknesses first.

A2.5.q: A business pays an outside consultancy to check and certify its network design before it is built. What is this?
A2.5.why: An outside expert reviews system designs before they are built.

A2.6.q: With permission, a security expert tries to break into a company's network and then writes up the weak spots found. What is this?
options: Hacking under the Computer Misuse Act
A2.6.why: Pen testing is an authorised simulated attack, ending in a report.

A2.7.q: A small firm decides that buying cyber insurance is cheaper than adding new security controls for one risk. What approach is this?
A2.7.why: Passive risk management transfers, avoids or accepts risk instead of adding controls.

A3.1.1.q: An online shop collects customer emails without consent and doesn't report a breach for two weeks. Which law has it broken?
A3.1.1.why: GDPR protects personal data and requires breaches to be reported within 72 hours.

A3.1.2.q: A student uses a teacher's password to get into the school system and change their marks. Which law has the student broken?
A3.1.2.why: The CMA makes unauthorised access to, and modification of, computer material a crime.

A3.3.1a.q: A gym asks members only for the details it actually needs and deletes them when membership ends. Which GDPR principles does this follow?
A3.3.1a.why: GDPR principles include collecting the minimum data, keeping it accurate and deleting it when done.

A3.3.1b.q: An employer processes staff bank details to pay their wages. Which lawful reason applies?
A3.3.1b.why: Processing needed to fulfil a contract, such as payroll, is a lawful reason under GDPR.

A3.3.1c.q: A customer asks a company to send them a copy of all the personal data it holds about them. Which right are they using?
A3.3.1c.why: GDPR gives people rights over their own data, including access and erasure.

A4.1.1.q: A data centre uses card entry, fingerprint scanners and locked server cabinets. Which type of measure is this?
A4.1.1.why: Physical measures protect equipment, sites and restricted areas.

A4.1.2.q: After ransomware hits, a company restores everything from last night's off-site copy and loses only a few hours of work. Which measure saved it?
A4.1.2.why: Backups let data be restored after loss, corruption or attack.

A4.1.3.q: Software spots a file that behaves suspiciously, even though it matches no known signature, and quarantines it. Which technique is this?
A4.1.3.why: Antivirus uses signatures for known malware and heuristics for suspicious behaviour.

A4.1.4.q: Rules are set to block all inbound traffic except on ports 443 and 25. Which measure is this?
A4.1.4.why: Firewalls filter traffic by rules to block unauthorised access.

A4.1.5.q: To log in, staff need their password and must also tap a USB security key. Which measure is this?
A4.1.5.why: MFA checks users are who they claim, using more than one factor.

A4.1.6.q: The finance team can open the accounts folder but not HR records. Which measure is this?
A4.1.6.why: Access controls decide which users can reach which resources.

A4.1.7.q: A TPM chip checks that a laptop's boot software hasn't been tampered with before it starts. Which measure is this?
A4.1.7.why: Trusted computing is hardware-based security. It adds protection but reduces user control.

A4.2.1.q: A stolen work laptop is useless to the thief because full-disk encryption makes the drive unreadable. Which type of encryption protected it?
A4.2.1.why: Storage encryption protects data at rest.

A4.2.2.q: Messages sent through an app are end-to-end encrypted, so an attacker who intercepts them sees only scrambled data. Which type of encryption is this?
A4.2.2.why: Communications encryption protects data in transit.

A4.3.q: An office upgrades its wireless security to WPA3 and changes the router's default admin password. What is it protecting?
A4.3.why: WLAN protection includes WPA3, changing default passwords and MAC filtering.

A4.4.q: Architects design a new system so every user gets only the access they need from day one, assuming attackers will try to get in. What principle is this?
A4.4.why: Security should be built in from the start, e.g. least privilege, not added later.
